query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated simulation approach that combines a quantum‐mechanical method for homogeneous alloy properties (such as the coherent potential approximation) with an actively learned machine‐learning interatomic potential (MTP) to explicitly account for local lattice relaxations and defect scattering (including oxygen-induced defects) will predict the temperature‐dependent low-frequency electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than conventional analytical models based on perfect, defect-free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk equimolar single-phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr alloy, either in its ideal defect-free state (for baseline comparisons) or with ~1 wt% oxygen impurity (as in experimental specimens).
generation.intervention: Introducing a simulation workflow that couples CPA electronic structure calculations with large-supercell simulations using actively learned MTPs to incorporate explicit atomic reconstructions around intrinsic and oxygen-induced defects.
generation.conditions: Two temperature regimes are considered: cryogenic temperatures (approximately 0–200 K) and elevated temperatures (approximately 300–1200 K).
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and defect clusters (including oxygen-induced precipitates or interstitials) that modify local electronic structure and scattering rates.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly modeling the local atomic relaxations and disorder caused by oxygen and other defects, the MTP-enabled supercell simulations capture enhanced electron scattering and modified relaxation times. These effects, when integrated with CPA’s treatment of the averaged electronic structure, adjust key parameters (such as the effective plasma frequency and electron relaxation time) used in conductivity calculations. This combined approach overcomes the limitations of analytical models that assume a perfect crystal lattice.
generation.predicted_outcome: The approach is predicted to reproduce a conductivity behavior that shows a relatively flat (or weakly varying) temperature dependence at low temperatures (0–200 K) due to suppressed phonon scattering and dominant defect scattering, and a gradual decline in conductivity from 300–1200 K as phonon contributions increase. Quantitatively, the predictive error relative to experimental measurements (with 1 wt% oxygen) is expected to be significantly lower (e.g., reduced by roughly 50% or more) than that achieved by conventional perfect-crystal analytical models.
generation.baseline: Predictions based on analytical models that use an ideal, defect-free crystal environment and neglect defect-induced scattering effects, which tend to misestimate the temperature dependence of conductivity.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be valid for temperatures from near absolute zero up to about 1200 K and for oxygen content near 1 wt%. It may become less accurate if additional phase transformations or extrinsic defect types arise outside these conditions.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on evidence from the ab initio framework employing CPA and actively learned MTPs for mechanical and electronic property predictions (e.g., as discussed in PMC11275555 and PMC8357793), and from studies on low-frequency conductivity modulated by relaxation time and plasma frequency (PMC11136967). The extension of those methods to reliably quantify defect scattering in conductivity predictions adds uncertainty, particularly regarding the precise magnitude of electron scattering effects introduced by oxygen and their temperature dependence.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples containing ~1 wt% oxygen. Measure their low-frequency electrical conductivity over two temperature regimes (0–200 K and 300–1200 K) using techniques such as terahertz spectroscopy and four-point probe measurements. Compare the experimental conductivity versus temperature curves with those predicted by (a) the integrated CPA+MTP approach and (b) traditional analytical models based on defect-free crystals.
measurements: Indicators of electron relaxation times and plasma frequencies via terahertz or complementary spectroscopic methods
Microstructure and defect characterization to confirm oxygen-induced disorder
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if (1) the integrated approach does not achieve a significantly lower (e.g., >50% improvement) predictive error relative to conventional analytical models when compared to the experimental data, or (2) if the predicted qualitative temperature dependence (i.e., a plateau at cryogenic temperatures and gradual decline at higher temperatures) markedly deviates from the measured behavior.

Compared with Fig. 2a, which shows the experimental results of resistivity as a function of thickness, it is obtained that when the Mo and W components are increased to 35%, the resistivity of the Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 film decreases, compared to the equimolar Nb25Mo25Ta25W25. Conversely, when Ta and W are increased to 35%, the resistivity of the Nb15Mo15Ta35W35 increases. This trend is consistent with calculation results in each thickness. It reveals that the resistivity of HEAs can be modulated by the inherent conductivity of the elements. Method 1 yields conductivity values that are approximately one order of magnitude higher than the experiment, indicating that applying the ideal solution concept, i.e., cocktail effect, to estimate conductivity in solid-solution HEAs can only provide a qualitative assessment. In conclusion, we have demonstrated how a combination of CPA and actively-learned MTPs can solve the problem of predicting the CRSS and intrinsic ductility of refractory MPEAs over the whole composition space with ab initio accuracy, a problem that is currently not tractable with conventional ab initio-based methods. In particular, by integrating our ab initio automated workflow into a robust Bayesian multi-objective optimization framework we have applied the developed approach to identifying high-performance Pareto-optimal compositions. Furthermore, our supercell size convergence tests enabled by MTP-powered molecular statics have revealed that sizes of typical supercell sizes used in conventional SQS calculations are often insufficient for accurate calculations of certain important materials properties, such as the surface energy, of multi-component alloys. Specifically, the surface energy of MoNbTi has been shown to exhibit a rather slow convergence with the supercell size, which leads to errors of 10–20% for SQS supercells of about 100 atoms.
